shots.narration: Scientists keep finding things in the ocean they wish they hadn't.
Doug is visiting every one of them, a little deeper each time.
Doug did not agree to this.
Sunlit.
The Sharkcano.
Off the Solomon Islands in the South Pacific, there is a volcano you usually can't see,
because its summit sits about twenty meters below the waves.
Twenty meters is about two school buses standing on end.
That's how close the top of this volcano comes to anyone swimming above it.
It's called Kavachi, and it is one of the most active underwater volcanoes in this part of the Pacific,
erupting on and off since at least nineteen thirty-nine.
In January twenty fifteen, the volcano went quiet for a while,
and a research team took the chance to drop cameras straight into the crater.
Here's the twist. The crater wasn't empty.
Scalloped hammerheads and silky sharks were swimming around inside it, along with a sixgill stingray.
That's the crater of an active volcano, and nobody knows whether they live there or slip in between eruptions.
The water in there gets hot and acidic, and the plumes carry sulfur and bits of volcanic rock.
One of the expedition scientists said there were plenty of reasons nothing should live in there except maybe bacteria.
Nobody knows how the sharks cope with any of it.
And it does erupt. In twenty twenty-two, satellites photographed it going off again,
with a cloud of hot, acidic, discolored water spreading across the surface above the crater.
Doug swims down and waves at a hammerhead, and the hammerhead is fine with it.
The volcano is not.
The sharks went straight back to circling,
like they have clearly seen this sort of thing before.
The Underwater Crop Circles.
In nineteen ninety-five, divers off Amami-Oshima, an island in southern Japan,
started finding perfect circles drawn in the sand of the seafloor.
Each one was about two meters across, about as wide as a bed is long,
with sharp ridges and valleys running out from the center like the spokes of a wheel.
They turned up ten to thirty meters down, perfectly symmetrical, and nobody could say who was making them.
It took until twenty eleven for researchers to finally catch the builder in the act.
It was a male pufferfish up to about twelve centimeters long, roughly the length of a phone,
and it was so new to science that it only got an official name in twenty fourteen.
The fish builds the whole thing by swimming along the seabed and flapping its fins against the sand,
digging valleys at different angles all the way around.
A single circle takes about seven to nine days of hard work.
Here's the disturbing part. The alien mystery was a fish trying to get a date.
The circle is a nest, and the females judge it.
The ridges and valleys gather fine sand into the middle,
and the researchers found the structure plays an important role in which male a female picks.
If she approves, she lays her eggs in the center.
And the male never reuses it, so next time he starts over and builds a brand-new one from scratch.
Doug builds a circle of his own right next door.
It's lopsided, and one side is a square.
Nobody comes.
Doug is used to this by now.
The Bottomless Blue Hole.
From a boat in Chetumal Bay, on the coast of Mexico,
it looks like a dark stain in the water.
In the Maya language, its name, Taam Ja', means deep water.
A blue hole is an underwater sinkhole, a shaft dropping straight down through the seafloor.
When this one was first measured in twenty twenty-one, it came out at about two hundred and seventy-five meters,
which was already close to the world record.
The record holder back then was the Dragon Hole in the South China Sea, at about three hundred meters,
and it's not a place anyone should want to visit.
Below about ninety meters, its water has no oxygen at all,
and the deeper part is full of hydrogen sulfide.
In December twenty twenty-three, the team came back to Taam Ja' with an instrument on a cable
that measures depth, temperature and saltiness as it sinks.
Here's the problem. The cable ran out before the hole did.
The instrument reached four hundred and twenty meters below sea level and still didn't touch the bottom.
That's deeper than the Empire State Building is tall to its roof.
Nobody knows how deep Taam Ja' goes.
Near the deepest readings, the water's temperature and saltiness looked a lot like the nearby Caribbean Sea,
which suggests the hole may connect to the open ocean through passages under the seabed.
Doug jumps in with a snorkel and a flashlight to find the bottom himself.
The beam goes down, and down, and down.
Only the cap comes back.
Doug didn't find the bottom either, but in fairness, neither did the scientists.
Pitch black.
The Lost City.
Most deep-sea vents are black chimneys pouring out water heated by magma.
This one is white, and nothing about it is volcanic.
In December two thousand, scientists exploring an underwater mountain in the middle of the Atlantic
stumbled onto a field of pale towers about seven hundred and fifty meters down.
They called it the Lost City.
The towers are almost pure carbonate, the same material as limestone.
The tallest one, named Poseidon, rises about sixty meters off the seafloor,
as tall as a twenty-story building.
Nothing down here is heated by a magma chamber.
Instead, seawater soaks into rock from Earth's mantle and reacts with it, slowly turning one mineral into another.
That reaction gives off heat, and it also releases hydrogen and methane, which the microbes living on the chimneys use as food.
The strange part comes from dating the oldest chimneys,
which shows the Lost City has been venting for about a hundred and twenty thousand years.
So the seafloor here has been making the raw ingredients of life out of plain rock,
with no sunlight and no volcano, for well over a thousand centuries.
Its discoverers think the first life on Earth may have started in a place a lot like this.
Doug climbs Poseidon to plant a flag on the top.
Limestone is not famous for holding up stick men.
A hundred and twenty thousand years of venting.
Poseidon lasted about four seconds with Doug on it.
The Bloop.
In the summer of nineteen ninety-seven, United States government hydrophones in the Pacific
picked up a sound so powerful it reached sensors more than five thousand kilometers apart.
That's farther than New York is from Los Angeles.
The ocean helps with that. In the tropics, about a kilometer down, sound travels at its slowest,
and low sounds get trapped in that layer like in a pipe, carrying for thousands of kilometers.
The recording rose quickly in pitch and was several times louder than a blue whale,
the loudest animal ever recorded.
It was nicknamed the Bloop,
and for a while even some of the researchers thought it was probably made by an animal.
It wasn't. The monster was ice.
The government's acoustics team later matched the Bloop to icequakes,
the sound of giant icebergs cracking and breaking apart,
most likely somewhere between the Antarctic Peninsula and the Ross Sea.
But that's not the disturbing part.
The same team has another sound on file, called the Upsweep,
and it was already there when they started listening in August nineteen ninety-one.
It peaks in spring and autumn,
and it comes from a remote part of the South Pacific, near an area of suspected volcanic activity.
More than thirty years later, its origin is still officially unresolved.
Doug goes monster hunting with a fishing rod,
and he stands on the nearest iceberg to get a better cast.
Doug found the monster.
He was standing on it.
The Jacuzzi of Despair.
About a thousand meters down in the Gulf of Mexico, there is a lake.
It has its own shore and its own surface,
and the scientists who found it picked that name on purpose.
A team led by Erik Cordes of Temple University found it in twenty fourteen
and came back the following year with a robot to take a closer look.
It's a brine pool.
The water inside is four to five times saltier than the sea around it,
which makes it heavy enough to sit on the bottom like a separate lake without mixing.
It's about thirty meters around and about four meters deep,
roughly the height of a double-decker bus.
Around its edge is a ring of mussels living off the gases that seep out of it.
The pool itself is loaded with methane and hydrogen sulfide, and there is no oxygen in it.
It's also warm, because the brine sits at about eighteen degrees Celsius, while the sea around it is about four.
The worst part is that warmth, because scientists think it may be what draws animals in.
Crabs wander over looking for food,
and whatever crosses the rim dies almost at once.
Then the salt preserves it.
Anything that falls in stays there, looking exactly as it did.
Doug sees warm water, a rim to sit on, and the word Jacuzzi.
He says nice, and gets in.
The cap floats on the surface, perfectly preserved.
The pool is very good at keeping things.
The Champagne Vent.
Plenty of underwater vents bubble gas.
In two thousand four, scientists found one in the western Pacific that bubbles liquid.
It sits on an underwater volcano called Northwest Eifuku, in the Mariana chain,
about one thousand six hundred meters down.
Streams of shiny droplets rise out of the seafloor like bubbles in a glass,
so the team named it Champagne vent.
But they aren't bubbles at all, they're drops of liquid carbon dioxide.
At that depth, the pressure is about one hundred and sixty times what it is at the surface,
roughly the weight of two grown men standing on every fingernail.
Under that much pressure, in water barely above freezing, carbon dioxide stays liquid,
and each drop grows a thin skin of hydrate, an ice-like cage of water and carbon dioxide.
The drops were so sticky that they clung to the robot like clumps of grapes.
And that's only the warm-up.
In the Okinawa Trough near Japan, about one thousand three hundred and eighty meters down,
scientists found an actual lake of liquid carbon dioxide trapped under the seafloor.
It's sealed in by a lid of the same ice-like hydrate,
and microbes live in the mud on top of it, sitting on a lake of something that should be a gas.
Doug brings two glasses and toasts the vent.
Nobody told him the fluid right next to the droplets comes out acidic,
at one hundred and three degrees Celsius.
The droplets kept rising toward the surface.
So did the cap.
The Scaly-Foot Snail.
Snails are not famous for their armor.
This one builds its own, out of iron.
It was discovered in two thousand one at the Kairei vent field in the Indian Ocean, almost three kilometers down.
Its foot is covered in overlapping scales,
and its shell and scales are coated in iron sulfide, the same family of minerals as fool's gold.
It's the only animal known to use iron as a major part of its skeleton.
An adult shell is usually about three centimeters wide, a little bigger than a quarter.
And it lives right beside black smokers,
where the water pours out at around three hundred and sixty degrees Celsius,
more than three times the boiling point of water at the surface.
What nobody expected was where the real threat would come from.
In twenty nineteen, it became the first animal ever listed as Endangered because of deep-sea mining.
It's known from only three vent fields in the whole ocean,
and two of them sit inside mining exploration licenses,
because the minerals around these vents contain valuable metals.
The assessment warned that even exploratory mining could damage the vents or smother the snails in sediment.
Doug tapes a saucepan to his chest to match the snail, and says hi.
Iron armor does nothing against three hundred and sixty degree water.
The snail is fine.
It has spent its whole life next to that vent, and it is not impressed.
Rock bottom.
The Asphalt Volcano.
In two thousand three, scientists found a volcano in the southern Gulf of Mexico, about three thousand meters down.
It erupts, but not with lava.
It's called Chapopote, and what comes out of it is asphalt, the same black, sticky stuff used to make roads.
It oozes out of the seafloor, then cools and hardens into flows with wrinkles and ropes,
so much like real lava that geologists compare the two directly.
It sits on the rim of a buried salt dome, surrounded by oil seeps and patches of frozen gas hydrate.
The hardened asphalt covers more than a square kilometer,
which is about a hundred and forty soccer fields of fresh tar.
You would expect a tar field three kilometers down, in total darkness, to be completely dead.
Instead, it was crowded.
Here's the part that should bother you. The tar itself is part of the menu.
Tubeworms grow out of cracks in the asphalt, with clams and other shellfish settled nearby.
The asphalt samples are partly digested,
and researchers found signs of oil-eating bacteria living right inside them,
while other microbes turn the oil into methane gas.
Life down here isn't just surviving next to the tar. It's slowly eating it.
And the team that found Chapopote thinks asphalt volcanoes like this one, with life like this on them, may be widespread deep in the Gulf.
Doug sees what looks like a freshly paved road and goes for a stroll.
It is a freshly paved road. He sticks.
The tubeworms didn't even look up.
Down here, a new shape in the tar is not news.
The Golden Orb.
On the thirtieth of August, twenty twenty-three, a robot exploring the Gulf of Alaska came across something nobody watching could name.
About three thousand two hundred and fifty meters down, a smooth golden dome was stuck to a rock.
It was about ten centimeters across, roughly the size of a grapefruit,
and it had a torn hole in its side.
The scientists watching the live video started guessing out loud.
Was it an egg case? A dead sponge?
They collected it and sent it to a lab, and for more than two years nobody could say for certain what it was.
Here's the twist, though. The answer turned out to be the least dramatic option available.
In April twenty twenty-six, scientists from the United States government and the Smithsonian announced it was dead tissue
from a giant deep-sea anemone whose tentacles can stretch to about two meters.
The orb was part of the base it uses to glue itself to rocks.
Doug pokes it with a stick, braced for the worst.
Nothing happens.
Doug is fine.
Two years of mystery, and nobody here is happy about how it ended.
Dark Oxygen.
Nearly all the oxygen made on Earth comes from living things using sunlight.
Four thousand meters down in the Pacific, there is no sunlight at all.
That's the floor of the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a deep plain between Hawaii and Mexico
that is about as wide as the continental United States.
It is covered in metal lumps called nodules, most of them about the size of a potato.
They contain nickel, cobalt, copper and manganese, metals used in batteries,
which makes this plain one of the biggest targets for deep-sea mining.
In twenty twenty-four, a team led by Andrew Sweetman reported something odd.
Sealed chambers they placed on this seafloor kept showing oxygen going up, in total darkness.
They proposed that the nodules act like natural batteries.
They measured up to about one volt on a single nodule,
and argued that clusters of nodules could split seawater into hydrogen and oxygen.
The catch is that nobody agrees it's real.
A mining company and several independent researchers published rebuttals arguing the rising oxygen came from the equipment, not the nodules.
The original team has since said the mechanism is still unclear,
and in April twenty twenty-six the journal added a note saying its editors are considering concerns about the paper.
For now, both sides want more measurements before anyone calls it settled.
Doug tries to charge his phone on a nodule.
One bar.
Then he tries to breathe the dark oxygen through his snorkel.
Doug has died. Again.
Even if dark oxygen is real, there was never going to be enough of it for Doug.
The Deepest Ecosystem Ever Found.
At the bottom of the deepest trenches there is no light, very little food drifts down from above, and the pressure is extreme.
You would expect almost nothing to live there.
Between July and August twenty twenty-four, the Chinese crewed submersible Fendouzhe made more than twenty dives
into the Kuril-Kamchatka Trench and the western Aleutian Trench, in the northwest Pacific between Russia and Alaska.
What the crew found was not empty.
The trench floor was covered in dense fields of tubeworms and clams,
and the crew kept finding them along about two thousand five hundred kilometers of trench,
roughly the distance from London to Moscow.
The communities ran from five thousand eight hundred meters all the way down to nine thousand five hundred and thirty-three meters.
That's deeper than Mount Everest is tall, with almost seven hundred meters to spare.
The pressure at the bottom is roughly nine hundred and fifty times what it is at the surface.
That's close to a tonne on every square centimeter,
about the weight of a small car on every fingernail.
None of this runs on sunlight.
Deep in the mud, microbes turn the remains of dead organic matter into methane.
That methane, along with hydrogen sulfide, seeps up through faults in the trench floor,
and bacteria living inside the tubeworms and clams turn those chemicals into food.
The unsettling part is how much of this we haven't seen.
These are the deepest communities of their kind ever recorded,
and the team thinks similar ones may be common in other trenches too, in places nobody has looked.
Doug has been this deep before. He brought back a plastic bag.
The gauge hits nine thousand five hundred and thirty-three meters.
Doug steps out of the submersible into a field of tubeworms and waves at a clam.
The pressure has been patient all episode.
Up on the ship,
the live feed shows the tubeworms swaying in the dark.
A red cap drifts into frame and settles among them,
and a clam closes on it.
Nine and a half kilometers down, the cap has finally found someone who wants to keep it.
Doug deaths: fifty-six.
Which deep-sea discovery should Doug visit next? Tell us in the comments.
